summary: A white cast-iron tower on a headland near King's Cove, Bonavista Peninsula, first lit 1893 or 1894. The Batterton family kept it until 1955; the Coast Guard owns it now, tower closed.

lens.note: Swedish Trotter-Lindberg revolving apparatus, first of its kind in Newfoundland (LighthouseFriends); the current light uses a Seagull 200mm lens (LighthouseFriends)

structures.note: Height from the Coast Guard List of Lights; Rowlett gives 11 m (36 ft)
Sold in 1935 and removed (LighthouseFriends); Rowlett says the keeper's house has been demolished

access.note: Grounds open; tower closed. Trail of about 1.7 km from the church in King's Cove.

events.note: Residents petition the Newfoundland government for a light at Western Point
Inspector John T. Nevill chooses Little Denier Island instead
Cast-iron tower erected (LighthouseFriends and Rowlett); the Heritage Character Statement gives 1894
Light first shown per LighthouseFriends and Rowlett; the Heritage Character Statement dates the build to 1894
Tower and store painted white after the 1896 inspection
Philip Batterton succeeds his father, who died in 1902
New occulting light, 14 s light and 6 s darkness, from 14 November 1929
Light changed to acetylene and listed as unwatched; keeper's post became caretaker
Keeper's dwelling sold to a family from Keels and removed
Maddox family takes over lightkeeping after James Batterton Jr. dies
Battery power from 1974; solar panel and batteries from 1984
Lightkeepers end; Canadian Coast Guard takes over the station

keepers.name: James Batterton
keepers.note: First keeper. Born Greenspond; lived in St. John's about fifteen years before King's Cove; earlier coxswain on the S.S. Plover under Captain Samuel Blandford. Spelled Batterton in LighthouseFriends.

keepers.name: Philip Batterton
keepers.note: Son of James Batterton; raised seven children at the station

keepers.name: James Batteron, Jr.
keepers.note: Caretaker of the unwatched light after his father's retirement (LighthouseFriends roster spells the name Batteron, Jr.)

keepers.name: Tom Walsh
keepers.note: Last lightkeeper; the Coast Guard took over the station in 2000

evidence.supports: James MacBraire set up premises at King's Cove in the early 1800s
evidence.quote: In the early 1800s, a St. John's merchant named James MacBraire established his major fishing premises at King's Cove.

evidence.supports: local young men trained in navigation; schooner captains
evidence.quote: During the winter, MacBraire took several local young men to St. John's to be trained in navigation, and as a result King's Cove developed a reputation for its successful schooner captains

evidence.supports: 1836 census population 413; Bonavista Bay about 5,000
evidence.quote: At the time of the first official Newfoundland census in 1836, King's Cove had a population of 413, which was significant as the total population of Bonavista Bay was only about 5,000.

evidence.supports: 1873 petition by J.C. Shears for a light at Western Point
evidence.quote: A petition from J.C. Shears and other residents of King's Cove calling for the erection of a lighthouse on King's Cove's Western Point was presented to the Newfoundland government in 1873

evidence.supports: 1887 Nevill chooses Little Denier Island; lit October 1888
evidence.quote: In 1887, Inspector John T. Nevill examined King's Cove and Little Denier Island and selected the latter. Little Denier Island Lighthouse commenced operation in October of 1888.

evidence.supports: King's Cove lighthouse received in 1893, cast-iron tower, cost $4,358.41
evidence.quote: King's Cove finally received a lighthouse in 1893, when a cast-iron tower was erected on Western Point at a cost of $4,358.41.

evidence.supports: Chance Brothers made the tower; sections shipped and assembled with riveted joints
evidence.quote: Designed and manufactured in the Chance Brothers factory in Birmingham, England, the separate sections for the tower were shipped to Newfoundland and assembled at King's Cove using overlapping riveted joints

evidence.supports: manufactured in Britain or from catalogue parts; Nevill probably overall designer
evidence.quote: Although the structure was manufactured in Britain, or assembled from parts ordered from a catalogue, there is increasing evidence to suggest that Nevill functioned as overall designer.

evidence.supports: heritage statement dates the lighthouse to 1894 under Nevill
evidence.quote: The lighthouse at King's Cove Head was built in 1894 under the direction of J.T. Nevill, Inspector of Lighthouses from 1871 to 1895.

evidence.supports: Rowlett gives 1893 and the focal plane and flash
evidence.quote: 1893. Active; focal plane 54 m (176 ft); white flash every 4 s.

evidence.supports: Rowlett: prefabricated by Chance Brothers; tower of cast iron
evidence.quote: The tower was prefabricated in England by Chance Brothers.

evidence.supports: Swedish Trotter-Lindberg revolving light, first of its kind in Newfoundland
evidence.quote: A Swedish Trotter-Lindberg revolving light, the first of its kind to be used in Newfoundland, was ordered for use at King's Cove

evidence.supports: screen made twelve revolutions a minute with two flashes each
evidence.quote: The screen at King's Cove made twelve revolutions per minute and produced two flashes per revolution

evidence.supports: focal plane of 54 metres
evidence.quote: The light had a focal plane of fifty-four metres.

evidence.supports: tower and store originally painted red; store 26.8 m from tower
evidence.quote: The tower was originally painted red, and a wooden store, also painted red, stood 26.8 metres from the tower.

evidence.supports: 1896 inspector recommends white paint; tower hard to see against pines
evidence.quote: The inspector also recommended that the tower be painted white, as it was hard to distinguish during the day against the dark background provided by the pine trees.

evidence.supports: tower and store painted white 1897; two-storey dwelling 1898
evidence.quote: The tower and store were painted white in 1897, and a new two-storey dwelling , also painted white, was built in 1898.

evidence.supports: inspector noted a small house beside the tower would be a convenience to the keeper (1896)
evidence.quote: small house, contiguous to the light-tower, would be a convenience to the keeper.

evidence.supports: Batterton born in Greenspond; lived in St. John's fifteen years
evidence.quote: Keeper James Batterton was born in Greenspond but had resided in St. John's for fifteen years prior to relocating to King's Cove.

evidence.supports: Batterton served as coxswain on the S.S. Plover under Captain Samuel Blandford
evidence.quote: Batterton had previously served as a coxswain aboard the S.S. Plover under Captain Samuel Blandford.

evidence.supports: Blandford appointed Batterton after election; local dismay; the local question
evidence.quote: was there not one man in King's Cove who could light a lamp?

evidence.supports: Evening Telegram death notice: widow of James Batterton (lighthouse keeper), 1926, four sons, one daughter, two stepdaughters
evidence.quote: Died - On Feb. 27th, at King's Cove, Annie, relict of the late James BATTERTON (Lighthouse Keeper), in her 86th year, leaving 4 sons, 1 daughter and 2 step-daughters.

evidence.supports: James Batterton died in 1902; son Philip succeeded
evidence.quote: James died in 1902 and his duties were passed down to his son Philip.

evidence.supports: Philip and his wife raised seven children at the lighthouse
evidence.quote: Philip and his wife raised seven children at the lighthouse.

evidence.supports: stable, pig barn, outhouse added; land cleared for vegetables
evidence.quote: A two-storey stable, a pig barn, and a double outhouse were added to the station, and the keeper and his family cleared land so vegetables could be cultivated.

evidence.supports: Philip retired 1933; James Jr. became caretaker
evidence.quote: Philip retired in 1933 and moved his family to St. John's, and his older brother, James Jr., who owned a home in King's Cove, became caretaker of the light.

evidence.supports: 1955 James Jr. died; lightkeeping passed to the Maddox family
evidence.quote: In 1955, James Jr. died, and the position of lightkeeper was passed to the Maddox family.

evidence.supports: keeper roster 1893 to 2000
evidence.quote: Keepers: James Batterton (1893 - 1902), Philip Batterton (1902 - 1933), James Batteron, Jr. (1933 - 1955), Thomas Maddox (1955 - 1974), Tom Maddox, Jr. (1974 - 1992 ), Tom Walsh (1992 - 2000).

evidence.supports: Walsh until 2000; lightkeeper tradition ended; Coast Guard took over
evidence.quote: Tom Walsh took over from 1992 until 2000, at which time the tradition of lightkeeper ceased and the lighthouse was taken over by the Canadian Coast Guard.

evidence.supports: 14 November 1929 occulting light, 14 s light and 6 s dark
evidence.quote: On November 14, 1929 a new and more powerful occulting light commenced operation at King's Cove with a characteristic of fourteen seconds of light followed by six seconds of darkness.

evidence.supports: 1931 acetylene; keeper becomes caretaker; unwatched light
evidence.quote: The job of keeper became that of a caretaker at this time as the acetylene light needed little maintenance and officially listed as an unwatched light.

evidence.supports: fog horn 1930 to 1940 to warn ships in foul weather
evidence.quote: a fog horn sounded from 1930-1940 to warn ships in foul weather.

evidence.supports: dwelling sold to the Murphys from Keels in 1935 and removed
evidence.quote: The keeper's dwelling on the point was sold to the Murphys from Keels in 1935 and removed by them.

evidence.supports: keeper's house demolished (Rowlett)
evidence.quote: The keeper's house has been demolished.

evidence.supports: battery power 1974 to 1984; solar collector from 1984
evidence.quote: Advances in technology permitted a change to battery power from 1974 to 1984.

evidence.supports: solar panel and batteries from 1984
evidence.quote: In 1984 a battery and solar collector power source was introduced.

evidence.supports: tower classified Recognized Federal Heritage Building in 1990
evidence.quote: The tower was classified a Recognized Federal Heritage Building in 1990.

evidence.supports: present light Fl W 4s, focal 53.6 m, range 5 nm, seasonal operation, tower 8.3 m
evidence.quote: Kings Cove Head Light 48 34 32.0 053 19 25.0 Fl W 4s 53.6 5 White cylindrical tower. 8.3 Seasonal. Flash 1 s; eclipse 3 s.

evidence.supports: Canadian Coast Guard owns; grounds open, tower closed
evidence.quote: The lighthouse is owned by the Canadian Coast Guard. Grounds open, tower closed.

evidence.supports: trail from the Saints Peter and Paul Church, about 1.7 km, roughly 45 minutes
evidence.quote: The 1.7 km, Inner Loop leads to the lighthouse and takes roughly 45 minutes.

evidence.supports: sound protective paint layer must be maintained
evidence.quote: a sound protective paint layer must be maintained

evidence.supports: lantern and weathervane focal point preserved without alteration
evidence.quote: The lantern and cap with its prominent weathervane is a focal point of the composition and should be preserved without alteration.

evidence.supports: about 26 prefabricated iron and steel lighthouses, the only surviving examples in Canada
evidence.quote: It is one of approximately 26 lighthouses of prefabricated iron and steel construction, thought to be the only surviving examples of their type in Canada.

evidence.supports: headland near the town of King's Cove
evidence.quote: Located on a headland near the town of King's Cove

evidence.supports: Bonavista Peninsula lighthouses section of the Rowlett directory
evidence.quote: The Bonavista Peninsula projects northeastward from the east coast of Newfoundland.

evidence.supports: plain white exterior of the tower (CRHP statement)
evidence.quote: the plain white exterior with no decoration.

evidence.supports: cast-iron construction, utilitarian structure (CRHP statement)
evidence.quote: is a very good example of a utilitarian structure of cast-iron construction

evidence.supports: Blandford appointed Batterton after his election for Bonavista
evidence.quote: Shortly after his election to the House of Assembly representing Bonavista, Blandford appointed Batterton as the first lighthouse keeper

evidence.supports: Mariners debated a light at Western Point or Little Denier Island
evidence.quote: there was a debate among mariners whether a light in Bonavista Bay would be best at Western Point or on Little Denier Island.

evidence.supports: heat from the flame turns the screen (Trotter-Lindberg)
evidence.quote: Under the Trotter-Lindberg system, the heat rising from the flame revolves a screen encircling the lamp to produce a flashing light.

evidence.supports: 1931 light source changed to acetylene gas
evidence.quote: The light source was changed to acetylene gas in 1931

evidence.supports: solar panel charges two lead-acid batteries that run the light automatically
evidence.quote: A 33 watt, 12 volt solar panel charges two lead acid batteries which run the light automatically.

evidence.supports: current light uses a Seagull 200mm lens
evidence.quote: The current light uses a Seagull 200mm lens and 0.77 ampere bulb.

evidence.supports: trailhead at the Saints Peter and Paul Church
evidence.quote: park at the Saints Peter and Paul Church, where you will find the trailhead

evidence.supports: site open, tower closed (Rowlett)
evidence.quote: Site open, tower closed.

corrections.why: The Coast Guard List of Lights gives 48 34 32.0 N, 053 19 25.0 W, and LighthouseFriends gives 48.57556, -53.32361. The OSM point is about 0.001 degrees of longitude east of both.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: LighthouseFriends and Rowlett give 1893; the Heritage Character Statement (1994) says the lighthouse was built in 1894 under Nevill. The story gives both and does not choose.

LighthouseFriends and Rowlett say Chance Brothers made the tower. The heritage statement says it was made in Britain or assembled from catalogue parts and that Nevill was probably the overall designer. Both are reported.
The Coast Guard list gives the structure as 8.3 m; Rowlett gives 11 m (36 ft); the brief's OSM-derived value is 8.0 m. The record keeps the Coast Guard figure pending a site check.

notes_for_editor: Dates disagree: 1893 (LighthouseFriends, Rowlett) against 1894 (heritage statement); the story gives both. Tower height disagrees: 8.3 m (Coast Guard list), 11 m (Rowlett), 8.0 m (brief). The brief's OSM position sits about 0.001 degrees east of the Coast Guard and LighthouseFriends positions. The Chance Heritage Trust page repeats LighthouseFriends almost word for word, so it is not counted as a separate source. The Find a Grave death notice is second-hand (Evening Telegram, 1 March 1926, as transcribed there); no copy of the newspaper was read. The heritage statement's reasons-for-designation paragraph names the Random Head Lighthouse, apparently a copy error from another statement; the King's Cove reading rests on the statement's heading and its 1894 date. Not reached: the Journal of the House of Assembly (1873 petition, 1887 Nevill report), the Board of Works tender records for 1893, the Evening Telegram, and the Parks Canada DFHD page (no readable text in the cache). Maddox, Maddox Jr., Walsh and Batterton Jr. are named only as the LighthouseFriends roster names them, in their keeper or caretaker role, with no personal detail.
